proof:
# One parity condition: full-body depth loss with a vanishing removed base mass

For every m,s>=1 and 0<epsilon<1/2 we construct a full-dimensional convex body with two sampling rules. With m integer coordinates its exact maximal depth is Gamma_s. Adding ONE integer-coordinate condition changes its exact maximal depth to Gamma_s/(2m). The coarse base marginal loses only its central atom, of mass 1/(2m+1). Thus the depth ratio tends to zero while that removed base mass tends to zero, although the arithmetic condition has index two after intrinsic lattice reduction.

The measure dimensions and admissible centers change. The body is NOT the convex hull of its fine mixed set. These qualifications are essential. The separate diamond-product examples retain the exact-fine-hull property.

## 1. A full-dimensional tube around the affine parity graph

Let

    Q_m={p in R^m:sum_i |p_i|<=1},
    P_m=Q_m intersect Z^m={0,+/-e_1,...,+/-e_m},
    g(p)=(1+sum_i p_i)/2.

Let K be a full-dimensional s-simplex of volume V and centroid c. Define

    C={ (p,u,x): p in Q_m, |u-g(p)|<=epsilon, x in K }
       subset R^m x R x R^s.                            (1)

This is a compact full-dimensional convex body. Indeed it is the invertible affine image of Q_m times [-epsilon,epsilon] times K under

    (p,t,x) -> (p,g(p)+t,x).

For the coarse rule only p is integer. All 2m+1 fibers are full-dimensional (s+1)-bodies

    [g(p)-epsilon,g(p)+epsilon] times K

of volume 2epsilon V. The coarse mixed measure is intrinsic H_(s+1), with total mass (2m+1)2epsilon V.

For the fine rule both p and u are integer. At p=0, the interval centered at 1/2 lies strictly between 0 and 1, so it contains no integer. At +e_i it is centered at 1 and contains exactly that integer; at -e_i it is centered at 0 and contains exactly that integer. Therefore the fine source has EXACTLY 2m positive fibers

    (+e_i,1):K,       (-e_i,0):K,

and no others. Its intrinsic dimension is s, and its total H_s mass is 2mV. No endpoint convention is hidden: epsilon<1/2 is strict.

## 2. Exact coarse maximum

At

    a_0=(0,1/2,c)

the normalized coarse source can be represented by independent random variables

    P uniform on P_m,
    T uniform on [-epsilon,epsilon],
    X uniform on K,
    U=g(P)+T.

A boundary-through-a_0 halfspace has scalar margin

    v dot (X-c) + (a+(b/2)1) dot P + bT.

The latter two terms form an independent symmetric additive noise Y. The proved paired-centroid-tail theorem and symmetric-noise corollary in `candidate 732b11a769399016` give probability at least Gamma_s when v!=0. If v=0, closed symmetry gives probability at least 1/2>=Gamma_s. A containing cap whose boundary misses a_0 can first be shifted to a_0, decreasing mass. Thus depth_coarse(a_0)>=Gamma_s.

For the matching global upper bound, the s+1 canonical simplex caps

    lambda_j(x)>=1/(s+1)

cover C and each captures exactly Gamma_s of the ENTIRE coarse measure: they ignore p and u. Consequently

    max coarse depth = Gamma_s.                         (2)

This is an all-normal statement. Its only additional analytic dependency is the already proved paired-tail theorem; no automatic product-depth preservation is assumed.

## 3. Exact fine maximum

Each fine base +/-e_i is exposed among the 2m positive bases by its signed coordinate normal. Its scalar value at its own point is 1, and at every other point it is at most 0. For the base p=sign*e_i, the actual ambient caps

    lambda_j(x)-1/(s+1)+2(sign*p_i-1)>=0                 (3)

isolate the canonical simplex caps at that base. They cover its whole K fiber, and each has fine mass exactly Gamma_s V. These finitely many caps cover all fine fibers and give global normalized depth at most Gamma_s/(2m).

At the own centroid of any fine fiber, every containing ambient halfspace captures at least Gamma_s V from that fiber by the ordinary simplex centroid bound (or the whole fiber if its x-normal is zero). Therefore

    max fine depth = Gamma_s/(2m).                      (4)

Equations (2)--(4) give the exact retention ratio

    max fine depth / max coarse depth = 1/(2m).          (5)

It tends to zero under one added integer condition, for fixed s and fixed epsilon, as m increases. This does not violate the true fine target Gamma_s/2^(m+1), which is at most (4).

## 4. What the removed-mass statement actually means

The coarse and fine measures have different intrinsic dimensions. In particular the fine source has zero H_(s+1) measure, so it is incorrect to identify (4) with retaining a positive fraction of the raw coarse volume.

There is nevertheless an exact common-space comparison. Project both normalized laws onto (p,x), forgetting u. Their projections are

    nu_coarse = Uniform(P_m) times Uniform(K),
    nu_fine   = Uniform({+/-e_i}) times Uniform(K).

The coarse BASE marginal atom omitted by fine sampling is precisely p=0, with mass 1/(2m+1). The projected normalized laws have total variation distance exactly

    ||nu_coarse-nu_fine||_TV = 1/(2m+1),                 (6)

where TV means the supremum over measurable sets. The discrepancy at p=0 is 1/(2m+1), and the total discrepancy on all other base atoms is the same, so half the L1 difference gives (6).

Despite this small projected-measure change, the center a_0 is no longer fine-admissible: there is no fine source point over p=0. The projected fine law is not the usual mixed-volume source of Q_m times K on the original lattice Z^m, because that body would contain the missing central fiber. Thus neither total-variation continuity with a fixed center domain nor an unchanged-lattice interpretation applies.

## 5. Lattice rank, index, and the exact-fine-hull limitation

The fine bases lie in the affine hyperplane

    2u-sum_i p_i=1.

Its affine integer lattice has rank m. Projection identifies it with the odd-parity coset in Z^m, of index two. The exact crosspolytope calculation in `candidate a67ad6a5110953aa` gives coarse base Helly number m+1 and filtered base Helly number 2m. Their ratio tends to two, but the ACTUAL coarse/fine depth ratio in (5) is unboundedly worse than a factor two. A bound on relative Helly numbers is not a relative retention theorem for the actual maximal depths.

The body (1) is full-dimensional, but

    conv(fine mixed set)
       = { (p,g(p),x):p in Q_m, x in K },                (7)

which has codimension one in C. Replacing C by this exact fine hull preserves every fine fiber and its depth, but collapses all coarse (s+1)-volumes to zero. A subsequent intrinsic lattice reduction keeps rank m and the odd-parity coset; it does not recover the old coarse source.

Accordingly this example refutes dimension-free depth retention based only on one added integer condition, its index two, and a vanishing removed BASE marginal mass. It does not refute a result additionally assuming a full-dimensional exact fine hull with controlled coarse sampling. The diamond products provide a different, precisely scoped obstruction under that stronger hull hypothesis.

`../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_one_parity_condition_depth_loss.py` checks the exact coarse/fine lattice slices, all cap gaps, rank/index basis, projected TV identity, and depth constants. The all-cap coarse lower bound is explicitly dependent on the proved paired-tail theorem.

# One parity condition: full-body depth loss with a vanishing removed base mass

**Full-dimensional parity tubes can lose arbitrarily much depth**

The full-dimensional parity-tube family in the source has exact coarse maximum depth Gamma_s and exact fine maximum depth Gamma_s/(2m); the projected-law total variation is 1/(2m+1). These equalities hold for all closed ambient halfspaces. Thus a single imposed parity condition can have arbitrarily poor depth retention despite small projected-law discrepancy.

Scope limits: Coarse and fine intrinsic dimensions and measures differ and are tracked separately; the fine hull has codimension one. This is not an OC counterexample.
